Code 56/5/2, 'CHEMISTRY (Theory)', Time 2 hours, Maximum Marks 35). ENGLISH = the EVEN indices 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 (folios 3, 5, 7, 9, 11). HINDI = the ODD indices 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 (folios 2, 4, 6, 8, 10). idx 11 (folio 12) is BLANK — a rule at the top, the footer '56/5/2  12' and a QR code, nothing else; CONFIRMED AT FULL SIZE rather than off the contact sheet, and there is no show-through ghost on it. The alternating hypothesis HELD exactly: I montaged the top ~21% of all five odd indices and every one opens in HINDI (idx 1 'सामान्य निर्देश', idx 3 Q5(क), idx 5 Q9(क), idx 7 'खण्ड ग' + the Hindi Q12 passage, idx 9 the Hindi Q12 (a)-(d)), so there is NO English overflow onto any odd top and no mid-paper parity inversion. English content runs continuously Q1 -> Q12: idx 2 = English General Instructions + SECTION A (Q1-Q3) + SECTION B start (Q4); idx 4 = Q5-Q8; idx 6 = Q9-Q11; idx 8 = SECTION C + Q12 lead-in, passage and cell diagram; idx 10 = Q12 sub-parts (a)-(d) and the (d) OR branch. Q12 is the only question split across a page boundary. ⚠ COVER vs FOLIO COUNT: the cover says 'contains 11 printed pages' while the booklet has 12 folios — the 12th is the blank one, so the cover is counting printed pages and is consistent; noted so nobody reads it as a missing page. ⚠ plan.txt for this paper reads 'no marking scheme found for 2022 56-5-2' and is WRONG (a stale Maths-pipeline artefact): the scheme is present at ms/p00..p05, six pages, and I confirmed it is THIS paper's by CONTENT and not by its footer — its Q2 answers Clemmensen (Zn-Hg/HCl) and Stephen (RCN + SnCl2 + HCl), matching the printed Q2, and its Q5(a)(i) answers 'Hexaammineplatinum (IV) chloride', matching the printed [Pt(NH3)6]Cl4. Header and footer both read 56/5/2 as well. STRUCTURE — read off the paper's own printed English General Instructions (idx 2) and it matches `term2_sci` EXACTLY, no disagreement: (1) 12 questions, all compulsory; (2) three sections A, B, C; (3) Section A = Q1-3, very short answer, 2 marks each; (4) Section B = Q4-11, short answer, 3 marks each; (5) Section C = Q12, case based, 5 marks; (6) log tables and calculators not allowed. 6 + 24 + 5 = 35, matching the cover's Maximum Marks 35 and the scheme's 'A full scale of marks 0-35 has to be used'. Row shape A3/B12/C5 = 20 rows, exactly the shape the addendum measured for term2_sci Chemistry. ⚠ ONE DISAGREEMENT WITH THE DISPATCH, and it is about the instruction COUNT, not the structure: the Maths brief says the internal-choice instruction 'is (vi) on a 2022 term2 paper, which prints only seven instructions in total'. This paper prints only SIX instructions and NONE of them mentions internal choice or gives a count — its (6) is the log-tables line. So the paper announces nothing about internal choice and the marking scheme is the only authority. NO MCQs anywhere — confirmed in both directions: I read all five English pages and there is not one four-option block, and the scheme has no Section-A letter table and no option letters in any of its six pages. Every row is `subjective`, no row carries an `answer`, and `audit:keys` has nothing to scan. This is the Chemistry half of the term2_sci subject split; had this been Physics, Q12 would have been five keyed MCQs. INTERNAL CHOICE — FIVE, established by walking the marking scheme question by question (ms/p02..p05) rather than by carrying a count over from a sibling. It reprints a bare 'OR' on its own line under Q4, Q5, Q9, Q11 and under sub-part Q12(d), and under NO other question; all five are independently confirmed by a printed 'OR' (and Hindi 'अथवा') on the paper itself at idx 2, 4, 6, 6 and 10. That is FIVE choices, ingested as paired rows with `_alternativeTo`, so the roster is asserted BY NUMBER and not inferred from the marks sum (which is structurally blind to a dropped alternative). Q6 prints (a) and (b) with '2+1=3' and NO 'OR', and the scheme gives both parts under one '6.' row, so Q6 is ONE question with two sub-parts; same for Q3 ('Do any two' of three sub-parts, scheme marks it '1x2 (Any two)'), Q1, Q2, Q7, Q8 and Q10. Note the choices sit on DIFFERENT question numbers from the opener 56/5/1, which chose Q5/Q6/Q9/Q11/Q12(d) — five each, but a roster carried over from it would have put an alternative on Q6 (which has none here) and missed Q4 (which does). ⚠ DECIMAL POINTS: this QUESTION PAPER prints ORDINARY BASELINE full stops, verified at 6x zoom on '1.5 M' and '138.9 S' in Q12(d)'s OR branch, where the decimal sits on the baseline and is indistinguishable from the sentence-final period beside it. So NO `{\cdot}` is used anywhere in this file. Its MARKING SCHEME disagrees with it and prints RAISED dots ('0·693', '138·9', '1·5', '0·208') — and is itself internally mixed, printing '2.303' with an ordinary dot on the same line as '0·693' — but the scheme is not transcribed, so nothing here is affected. questions._figure: REQUIRED — 'silver plate' appears NOWHERE in the passage; it is a label on the drawn cell, so without the figure the stem names a referent the reader has never met. The drawing shows two beakers, I on the left with a zinc plate in a \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}(aq)}\) solution and II on the right with a silver plate in \(\mathrm{Ag^{+}(aq)}\), joined by a salt bridge and by an external wire through a voltmeter. Page idx 8.
questions.context:
Oxidation-reduction reactions are commonly known as redox reactions. They involve transfer of electrons from one species to another. In a spontaneous reaction, energy is released which can be used to do useful work. The reaction is split into two half reactions. Two different containers are used and a wire is used to drive the electrons from one side to the other and a Voltaic/Galvanic cell is created. It is an electrochemical cell that uses spontaneous redox reactions to generate electricity. A salt bridge also connects to the half cells. The reading of the voltmeter gives the cell voltage or cell potential or electromotive force. If \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{cell}}\) is positive the reaction is spontaneous and if it is negative the reaction is non-spontaneous and is referred to as electrolytic cell. Electrolysis refers to the decomposition of a substance by an electric current. One mole of electric charge when passed through a cell will discharge half a mole of a divalent metal ion such as \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\). This was first formulated by Faraday in the form of laws of electrolysis.
The conductance of material is the property of materials due to which a material allows the flow of ions through itself and thus conducts electricity. Conductivity is represented by k and it depends upon nature and concentration of electrolyte, temperature etc. A more common term molar conductivity of a solution at a given concentration is conductance of the volume of solution containing one mole of electrolyte kept between two electrodes with the unit area of cross-section and distance of unit length. Limiting molar conductivity of weak electrolytes cannot be obtained graphically.
questions.stem: Is silver plate the anode or cathode?

questions._figure: REQUIRED — 'the salt bridge' is definite and points at the one drawn between beakers I and II; the passage mentions a salt bridge only in the abstract. questions.context:
Oxidation-reduction reactions are commonly known as redox reactions. They involve transfer of electrons from one species to another. In a spontaneous reaction, energy is released which can be used to do useful work. The reaction is split into two half reactions. Two different containers are used and a wire is used to drive the electrons from one side to the other and a Voltaic/Galvanic cell is created. It is an electrochemical cell that uses spontaneous redox reactions to generate electricity. A salt bridge also connects to the half cells. The reading of the voltmeter gives the cell voltage or cell potential or electromotive force. If \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{cell}}\) is positive the reaction is spontaneous and if it is negative the reaction is non-spontaneous and is referred to as electrolytic cell. Electrolysis refers to the decomposition of a substance by an electric current. One mole of electric charge when passed through a cell will discharge half a mole of a divalent metal ion such as \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\). This was first formulated by Faraday in the form of laws of electrolysis.
